methods.label: Hexagon and circular sectors
methods.explanation:
Use the regular hexagon as a starting region, then add the outward circular pieces and subtract the inward ones. Label its marked centers \(A,B,C,D,E,F\) clockwise, beginning at the top. The outward lobes are centered at \(A,C,E\), each using two arcs along the major circular path. The inward arcs are centered at \(B,D,F\).

[Figure 1](figures/2012_AMC_10A_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

First establish the common radius \(r>0\) and the central angle \(\theta\) of one arc. The arc-length formula gives
\[
\frac{\theta}{360^\circ}\,2\pi r=\frac{2\pi}{3},
\qquad \theta=\frac{120^\circ}{r}.
\]
Circles centered at adjacent hexagon vertices share an arc junction. Their centers are distance \(2\) apart, so the triangle inequality gives \(2\le 2r\). Thus \(r\ge1\) and \(\theta\le120^\circ\). Each outward lobe follows a major arc of angle \(2\theta\), so \(\theta>90^\circ\) and \(r<4/3\).

Suppose \(r>1\). Joining adjacent centers to their shared junction forms an isosceles triangle with sides \(r,r,2\). All these triangles are congruent; let their common base angle be \(\alpha>0\). An altitude splits such a triangle into right triangles with legs \(1\) and \(\sqrt{r^2-1}<1\), so \(\alpha<45^\circ\).

Each hexagon interior angle is \((6-2)180^\circ/6=120^\circ\). At an inward center, each endpoint radius tilts by \(\alpha\) from the direction toward its neighboring center. Opposite tilts leave a \(120^\circ\) angle. Tilts that widen the angle give a short circular path greater than \(120^\circ\), because \(\alpha<45^\circ\). Therefore, to obtain \(\theta<120^\circ\), both radii must tilt toward each other, giving
\[
\theta=120^\circ-2\alpha.
\]
Since \(\theta>90^\circ\), this also gives \(\alpha<15^\circ\). At an outward center, the possible major-path angles are consequently \(240^\circ-2\alpha\), \(240^\circ\), and \(240^\circ+2\alpha\). Since \(2\theta<240^\circ\), we must have
\[
2\theta=240^\circ-2\alpha.
\]
Doubling the preceding equation for \(\theta\) instead gives \(2\theta=240^\circ-4\alpha\), forcing \(\alpha=0\), a contradiction. Hence \(r=1\) and \(\theta=120^\circ\). Adjacent circles are therefore tangent at the side midpoints.

Connecting the hexagon's center to its vertices divides it into six equilateral triangles of side \(2\). Each has height \(\sqrt{2^2-1^2}=\sqrt3\) and area \(\sqrt3\), so the hexagon's area is \(6\sqrt3\).

At each of \(A,C,E\), add the outward \(240^\circ\) sector, of area \(2\pi/3\). At each of \(B,D,F\), remove the inward \(120^\circ\) sector, of area \(\pi/3\). These pieces have disjoint interiors because the unit-circle centers are at least \(2\) apart. The enclosed area is
\[
6\sqrt3+3\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)
-3\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)
=\boxed{\pi+6\sqrt3},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
